The Aerosense measurement system uses low-cost, low-power MEMS sensors to measure local pressures, blade motions, and inflow conditions on wind turbine rotor blades.
The system is composed of sensor nodes installed on the blades, a base station that collects and transmits the data, and a digital twin system for data processing and analysis.
The pressure distribution is measured using an array of 40 absolute pressure sensors, while 5 differential pressure sensors measure the pressure difference around the leading edge.
A 9-axis inertial measurement unit is used to measure the blade motion and attitude, which is necessary to correct the pressure measurements for hydrostatic and acceleration effects.
Careful calibration of the absolute pressure sensors was required to achieve an accuracy of 1% of the full-scale pressure range.
Photogrammetry was used to measure the 3D shape and sensor positions on the blade section, which is necessary to compute the integrated aerodynamic forces.
Experiments on a 7kW wind turbine showed that the pressure distribution can vary significantly during a single rotation of the blade, even under stable wind conditions.
These variations were found to be due to the misalignment of the wind direction with the wind turbine's rotational axis.

The Aerosense system was able to infer the local inflow conditions using a hybrid method that combines the differential pressure measurements with inviscid flow theory, without requiring a reference pressure measurement.

The orders of magnitude for the different types of pressure measured on a 5MW wind turbine are: dynamic pressure ~2000 Pa, atmospheric pressure ~100,000 Pa, hydrostatic pressure variation ~800 Pa, and pressure drift ~100 Pa/year.
Previous field measurement campaigns required complex and costly instrumentation embedded inside the rotor blades, with long pressure tubes that limited the measurement frequency.
In contrast, the Aerosense system is wireless, self-sufficient, less complex, and less costly, while also allowing higher measurement frequencies to capture unsteady aerodynamic effects.
The Aerosense system was designed to be easy to install, inexpensive, and non-intrusive, making it a cost-effective solution for the wind energy industry.
The digital twin system integrated with the Aerosense measurement data allows for automated data processing, analysis, and comparison with simulations.
The Aerosense system has the potential to provide valuable insights into the aerodynamic behavior of wind turbine rotor blades, which can be used to improve their design and performance.
